blocks.text: Abstract

Britain is connecting tens of gigawatts of data-centre and energy load to a grid that can no longer promise to keep it switched on. The connections that clear the queue fastest are non-firm — interruptible, curtailable, flexible by contract — and that interruptibility is a genuine, recurring loss driver. Yet almost no one in the insurance market prices it. Property and business-interruption wordings were written for damage; a grid operator lawfully curtailing a connection is not damage.{{cite:ACAD-CRI-GRID-SRI,LMA-BI-GUIDE}} The risk is real, it is growing, and it is being carried blind.

The Non-Firm Power Risk Index is an outside-in attempt to make that exposure legible. It scores the UK insurance-market participants standing in the path of interruptible-power risk — carriers and Lloyd's syndicates, MGAs and brokers, the underlying energy and data-centre assets, and the reinsurers behind them — on two axes, and reduces each to a single number you can rank.

The argument in brief: the peril is large and structurally unpriced; the catastrophe and cyber models the market would reach for cannot see it, because each is built around the wrong correlation substrate; and pricing it correctly needs a new primitive — not a hazard score but a Margin of Safety, preparedness minus exposure. On the current provisional slice the data already shows the two coming apart, which is the whole reason a one-axis score would mislead. The analysis that follows makes each step of that case in turn, then hands you the live index to test it.
Why now

What changed is the load. A factory drawing power on a nine-to-five shift could absorb an overnight curtailment; an AI training cluster cannot. Compute is a 24/7, always-on consumer that monetises every hour and contracts to do so — so for the first time the demand side is paying a premium for firmness itself, and the data-centre build-out has put that always-on load at the front of a grid that can no longer promise it.{{cite:INDUSTRY-DC-COMPUTE-DEMAND,ACAD-CCM-NF-LOAD}} Non-firm risk is not an old peril rediscovered; it is a new one, created by the collision of an always-on demand curve with an interruptible grid. The market has not repriced for it. This index is, at bottom, a claim that it should — that the risk is real, measurable, and currently underpriced, and that whoever measures it first is positioned to price it.{{cite:NESO-CONSTRAINT-COSTS}}
The frame
Exposure against Preparedness

Every entity is placed on two scored axes. Exposure measures the size of the bet: how much non-firm, curtailable load sits in the book or the asset, how concentrated it is on the same grid geography, and how badly today's wordings miss the peril. Preparedness measures the ability to carry it: whether the underwriter has the data, the products, the modelling, the expertise and the capital to actually hold the risk it has written.

Margin of Safety = Preparedness − Exposure. The market deploys capacity onto whoever looks exposed — but losses concentrate where exposure has run ahead of preparedness, while the genuinely capable sit in under-priced whitespace.

blocks.caption: The two axes cut the field into four quadrants. The warning light is a large negative margin.

cells.label: Whitespace
cells.note: Capable, under-deployed. Capacity is available here but not yet earning — the opportunity.

cells.label: Earning it
cells.note: Exposed and prepared. Carrying real non-firm risk with the data, products and capital to match.

cells.label: Sidelined
cells.note: Neither exposed nor ready. Watching from the bench while the market forms.

cells.label: Exposed
cells.note: Exposure accumulating faster than the data, products and capital to support it. The danger zone.

blocks.text: Why an index
A wedge, not a data vendor

A risk score, sold as a score, is a weak business — it productises one number and waits for a buyer. That is not the point of this index. The index is a wedge: the proprietary, primary-source understanding of a peril that the rest of the market underwrites blind. The discipline that builds the index — reconciling connection registers, capacity filings, ratings and wordings down to a single comparable picture — is the same discipline that lets you actually price the gap and carry it.

The measured features are built to be exactly that edge: connection-gate status from the grid operator, the flexible-connection share from the distribution registers, aggregation over shared grid geography, and the distance between the physical-damage cover the market sells today and the parametric availability cover the risk actually needs. Whoever holds that picture first is positioned not to sell a score, but to write the cover that does not yet exist — a parametric non-firm availability cover that pays on lost grid availability rather than physical damage, priced off the Margin of Safety. The Product section sets it out in full.
The discipline
No synthetic data

An AI-scored index is only worth the rigour underneath it. Every rating in NFRI carries an evidence tier — measured (a register), disclosed (a filing or rating), derived (computed from those), or assessed (sourced research judgement). Scoring is arithmetic in code, never an LLM opinion: ratings fuse a latent research judgement with a deterministic register/filing reading by credibility weighting.{{cite:ACT-CREDIBILITY}} A publication gate holds the whole index at PROVISIONAL until at least 60% of the blended score rests on measured or disclosed evidence. Until the live registers and filings land, the direction is defensible and the magnitudes are honest estimates — and the banner says so.
This is the doloop discipline applied to a research index: show what is actually in force, mark what is assessed, and refuse to dress a prior up as a measurement.
How to read it

Below: the live index. Each dot is an entity, placed by its Exposure and Preparedness scores; size is data confidence, and the fill shows how much of the score rests on measured evidence. Dashed lines are the median cut-points that define the quadrants. Click any point — or any row in the ranked table — to open the full decomposition: every sub-factor, its latent and deterministic ratings, its evidence tier, and the citation behind it.
